summary: Kentucky's Safe at Home Program, in the Secretary of State's office, is meant to protect victims of sexual assault, rape, other sexual crimes, domestic violence, human trafficking, and stalking. It lets victims, their minor children, and everyone who lives with them use a designated address. It is open to victims who are U.S. citizens and Kentucky residents, at no cost to them.
quote: The Safe at Home Program is hereby established within the Office of the Secretary of State. The Safe at Home Program shall be operated with the intent to protect victims of: (a) Domestic violence; (b) Human trafficking; (c) Stalking; (d) Sexual assault; (e) Rape; and (f) Other sexual crimes as defined by KRS 17.500. The Safe at Home Program shall authorize the use of designated addresses for victims, their minor children, and all other individuals residing with the victim. The Safe at Home Program shall be open to victims of a specified offense who are United States citizens and residents of Kentucky, without any cost to the program participant.
source_title: KRS 14.302 (Safe at Home Program established, designated addresses)

summary: While an application is pending, the board can make an emergency award of up to $1,000 if a final award is likely and the claimant would face undue hardship without quick help. (c) An attestation from a healthcare provider who conducted an examination of the personal injury suffered by the victim. summary: The fund is the payer of last resort and pays crime-related out-of-pocket costs that insurance and other sources do not cover.

summary: For a sexual assault victim, the board may not deny or reduce an award based on things like how the victim was dressed, where they were, alcohol or drug use, a prior relationship with the offender, or living with the offender afterward.

source_title: LAC Title 22, Part XIII, Crime Victims Reparations Board rules (Feb 2025)

source_title: LAC Title 22, Part XIII, Crime Victims Reparations Board rules (Feb 2025)

source_title: LAC Title 22, Part XIII, Crime Victims Reparations Board rules (Feb 2025)

summary: For outstanding medical bills, the board pays up to 70 percent of what is left after insurance and other third-party payers, within the award limits.
quote: The board will pay up to 70 percent of all outstanding charges after any third-party payment sources up to the statutory limits.
source_title: LAC Title 22, Part XIII, Crime Victims Reparations Board rules (Feb 2025)

summary: Medical costs the victim already paid out of pocket are reimbursed before the percentage schedule for unpaid bills is applied.

source_title: LAC Title 22, Part XIII, Crime Victims Reparations Board rules (Feb 2025)

summary: Lost wages are paid at 80 percent of the victim's gross weekly wage, or 80 percent of the average weekly wage for seasonal or part-time work.
quote: 80 percent of the gross weekly wage of the victim. For seasonal or part time wages, the amount shall be calculated at 80 percent of the average weekly wage;
source_title: LAC Title 22, Part XIII, Crime Victims Reparations Board rules (Feb 2025)

summary: Moving costs are paid only when the claimant must move because of the crime for reasons of imminent danger, personal safety, or a threat of injury, up to $5,000 per household. The board rule says a police or incident report should be sent with the claim to show why the move was needed.

source_title: LAC Title 22, Part XIII, Crime Victims Reparations Board rules (Feb 2025)

summary: Cleaning the victim's residential crime scene is capped at $2,500.

source_title: LAC Title 22, Part XIII, Crime Victims Reparations Board rules (Feb 2025)

summary: Public agencies, including the crime victims compensation board by name, may not publicly disclose the name, address, contact information, or identity of sex offense victims. The victim can waive this.
quote: all public officials and officers and public agencies, including but not limited to all law enforcement agencies, sheriffs, district attorneys, judicial officers, clerks of court, the Crime Victims Reparations Board, and the Department of Children and Family Services or any division thereof, shall not publicly disclose the name, address, contact information, or identity of crime victims who at the time of the commission of the offense are minors under eighteen years of age or of victims of sex offenses
source_title: La. R.S. 46:1844, Basic rights for victim and witness (2025 text, Justia)

summary: Hospitals may not bill sexual assault exam patients for co-payments or other costs tied to their own health insurance; those amounts go to the state victim compensation program instead.

source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

summary: Victim compensation can cover the forensic exam and other emergency department costs whether or not the survivor reports to police.

source_title: Mass.gov DPH, MA SANE Protocol Section X: Victim Compensation

source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

summary: The maximum award is $25,000 per claimant, or $50,000 for a catastrophic injury.
quote: The maximum award for compensation to a claimant pursuant to this chapter shall be $25,000; provided, however, that the maximum award for compensation to a claimant with a catastrophic injury pursuant to this chapter shall be $50,000.
source_title: M.G.L. c. 258C, s. 3, Maximum award; compensable expenses

summary: A victim, or a family member living with the victim, can be compensated for security measures up to $3,000.
quote: A victim or a family member residing with the victim at the time a crime is committed, shall be eligible for compensation for the costs associated with the implementation of security measures; provided, however, that the maximum compensable amount shall not exceed $3,000.
source_title: M.G.L. c. 258C, s. 3, Maximum award; compensable expenses

summary: Clothing and bedding seized as evidence or ruined by the investigation can be replaced up to $250.
quote: A victim shall be eligible for compensation for the reasonable replacement costs of clothing and bedding seized as evidence or rendered unusable as the result of a criminal investigation that is the direct result of a crime; provided, however, that the maximum compensable amount shall not exceed $250.
source_title: M.G.L. c. 258C, s. 3, Maximum award; compensable expenses

summary: Professional crime scene cleanup at a private residence or a victim's vehicle is capped at $1,500.
quote: Expenses incurred for professional crime scene cleanup services necessary as the direct result of the commission of a crime at a private residence or in a motor vehicle that is owned or leased by a victim, family member or other dependent shall be compensable in accordance with this chapter; provided, however, that the maximum amount of compensation shall not exceed $1,500.
source_title: M.G.L. c. 258C, s. 3, Maximum award; compensable expenses

summary: Funeral and burial expenses are capped at $13,000.
quote: The maximum award or compensation for funeral and burial expenses shall be $13,000.
source_title: M.G.L. c. 258C, s. 3, Maximum award; compensable expenses

summary: If an attorney helps with the claim, fees are paid at no more than $75 per hour, capped at 15% of the award, and come out of the award rather than on top of it.
quote: Attorneys shall be compensated at a rate of no more than $75 per hour. In no event shall an attorney's fee award exceed 15% of the total award for compensation.
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

summary: A victim, or a parent or guardian of a minor victim, can be compensated for reasonable mental health counseling obtained because of the crime.
quote: A victim, parent or legal guardian of a victim who is a minor in accordance with section 4 or, where death results from the crime, the dependents and family members of the victim, shall be eligible for compensation for reasonable mental health counseling obtained as a result of the crime.
source_title: M.G.L. c. 258C, s. 3, Maximum award; compensable expenses

summary: Physician, dental, ambulance and other medically necessary services caused by the crime are covered when the claimant shows an out-of-pocket loss or a legal liability to pay.
quote: Expenses incurred for physician, dental, ambulance, or other medically necessary services or prosthetic devices as the direct result of injury to the victim shall be compensable in accordance with this chapter; provided however, that when claiming compensation for such expenses, the claimant must demonstrate an out-of-pocket loss or legal liability for payment of such expenses.
source_title: M.G.L. c. 258C, s. 3, Maximum award; compensable expenses

summary: A victim who was employed, or had a real job offer, can be compensated for lost earnings while medically disabled from work because of the crime, based on net earnings.
quote: If the victim was employed or had received a bona fide employment offer at the time of the crime, the victim shall be eligible for compensation for loss of actual earnings due to disability from work as the result of injuries caused by the crime.
source_title: M.G.L. c. 258C, s. 3, Maximum award; compensable expenses

summary: Transportation to medical care is covered only for ambulance, chair car, dial-a-ride, taxi or rideshare costs.
quote: Compensation for transportation costs incurred while obtaining medical care is limited to costs incurred for emergency and non-emergency ambulance service, chair car service, dial-a-ride, taxi, or ridesharing service obtained.
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

summary: Security measures can include doors, locks, exterior windows, security systems and reprogramming security codes.
quote: Security measures may include but are not limited to, external and internal doors and locks, exterior windows and locks, security systems, and reprogramming security codes.
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

params: {"expense":"property_replacement","item":"Property losses, pain and suffering, and all other losses not listed as covered"}
summary: The program page lists property losses, pain and suffering, and all other losses outside the covered list as not covered. The only property-type item on the covered list is replacement of clothing and bedding taken as evidence or ruined by the investigation.
quote: Property losses, compensation for pain and suffering, and all other losses
pinpoint: MOVA, Applying for Victims of Violent Crime Assistance, What expenses are not covered?
source_title: Mass.gov, Applying for Victims of Violent Crime Assistance (MOVA)

params: {"item":"Public transportation, and mileage or parking when private transportation is used"}
summary: Bus or train fares, and mileage or parking for a personal car, are not reimbursed for trips to medical or mental health care.
quote: It does not include compensation for public transportation, or mileage or parking when private transportation is used.
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

params: {"item":"Missed or cancelled counseling appointments, non-therapeutic court appearances and consultations, photocopying and report writing"}
summary: Counseling compensation may be denied for missed or cancelled appointments and for non-therapeutic court or investigative work by the provider.
quote: Compensation for mental health counseling may be denied for expenses incurred in the following instances: 1. missed or cancelled appointments; 2. non-therapeutic testimonial court appearances by a health care provider; 3. non-therapeutic investigatory consultations; 4. photocopying and report writing;
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

summary: A claim must be filed within three years of the date of the crime.
quote: A claim for compensation under this chapter shall be filed within three years of the date of the crime.
source_title: M.G.L. c. 258C, s. 5, Filing and proof of claims

params: {"years":3,"from":"age_18","extension":"Applies when the victim was a minor at the time of the crime; does not apply to claims based on the death of a minor victim."}
summary: If the victim was a minor, the three-year filing period does not start until the victim turns 18.
quote: The three-year filing period shall not commence until the victim reaches the age of 18.
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

summary: If the victim was a minor and a criminal complaint or indictment came after the victim turned 18, the time to file starts on the date it was issued.
quote: If the victim was a minor when the crime was committed and the crime results in the issuance of a criminal complaint or indictment after the victim's 18th birthday, the filing period shall not commence until the date of issuance of the criminal complaint or indictment provided, however, that this exception shall not apply to claims based on the death of a minor victim.
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

params: {"years":3,"from":"discovery","extension":"Only if the crime resulted in a criminal complaint, indictment, or other judicial or administrative probable cause determination."}
summary: If you did not discover the crime until more than 3 years after it happened, the 3 years start when you discovered it, or should have. This applies only if there was a criminal complaint, an indictment, or another finding of probable cause.
quote: If the claimant did not discover the act which constitutes a crime until more than three years after the crime was committed, the filing period shall not commence until the claimant discovered, or reasonably should have discovered, the act which constitutes a crime; provided, however, that in such cases, the crime for which the claimant seeks compensation must have resulted in the issuance of a criminal complaint or indictment, or any other judicial or administrative determination of probable cause that an act constituting a crime has occurred.
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

params: {"required":true,"within_days":5,"exception":"or later if the program finds good cause or you were under 18"}
summary: The crime must be reported within five days unless the agency finds good cause for the delay. Victims under 18 are not held to the five-day limit.
quote: Except in the case where the agency finds such report to have been delayed for good cause, such report shall have been made within five days after the occurrence of such crime; provided, however, that a claimant who was a victim under 18 years of age shall not be required to file such report within 5 days.
source_title: M.G.L. c. 258C, s. 2, Eligibility for compensation

summary: A Provider Sexual Crime Report filed by a medical provider counts as a report to law enforcement.
quote: Reports to local law enforcement, via a Provider Sexual Crime Report (PSCR), in accordance with M.G.L. c. 112, § 12A½, shall constitute a report to law enforcement authorities.
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

summary: Applying to a court for a restraining or harassment prevention order with a supporting affidavit, or applying for a criminal complaint, counts as a report to law enforcement.
quote: The reporting of a crime to a court through a citizen application for a restraining order under M.G.L. c. 209A, and M.G.L. c. 258E, accompanied by an affidavit in support of the application for protection, or through a citizen application for a criminal complaint, shall constitute a report to law enforcement authorities.
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

summary: Telling a rape crisis center, private security, or the agency itself does not count as a report to law enforcement.
quote: Reports to private security personnel, rape crisis centers, or the Agency do not constitute reports to law enforcement authorities.
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

summary: Good cause for a late report includes physical or psychological incapacity, or reasonable fear for the safety of the victim or others.
quote: Good cause for delay shall include delay caused by physical or psychological incapacity which prevented the making of a report; or by (c) reasonable fear of safety for themselves or others.
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

summary: For a minor victim, a report to the Department of Children and Families under the state's mandated child abuse reporting law counts as a report for compensation purposes.
quote: Crimes involving minor victims may be reported to the Department of Children and Families pursuant to the reporting requirements of M.G.L. c. 119, § 51A.
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

summary: To get compensation, the claimant must cooperate with law enforcement in the investigation and prosecution of the crime. This does not apply if the claimant shows a reasonable excuse for not cooperating.
quote: A claimant shall be eligible for compensation only if such claimant cooperates with law enforcement authorities in the investigation and prosecution of the crime in which the victim was injured or killed unless the claimant demonstrates that he possesses or possessed a reasonable excuse for failing to cooperate.
source_title: M.G.L. c. 258C, s. 2, Eligibility for compensation

summary: The program may accept the physical or psychological effects of the crime as a reasonable excuse for not cooperating. A reasonable fear for the safety of the claimant or others can count too.
quote: The Agency may find that the physical or psychological impact of the crime and/or a reasonable fear of safety for themselves or others shall constitute a reasonable excuse and shall not constitute lack of cooperation.
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

summary: The program pays only for losses not covered by insurance, public benefits, restitution, civil suits or institutional gifts.
quote: No compensation shall be awarded or paid unless the out-of-pocket expenses or legal liability of the claimant for services rendered as the result of the crime exceeds any and all of the amounts received, applied for, or to be applied for as the result of the crime from any of the following or any combination of the following:
source_title: M.G.L. c. 258C, s. 10, Amounts received by claimant from other sources; offset

summary: Crowdfunding raised for a victim does not have to be reported and is not treated as a source that must be used first.
quote: Claimants have no obligation to notify the Agency of crowd funding dollars raised on their behalf, as this funding will not be considered as a source of payment that must be exhausted
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

summary: An award may be reduced or denied to the extent the victim's conduct provoked or contributed to the injuries.
quote: To the extent that the victim's acts or conduct provoked or contributed to the injuries, the agency may reduce or deny an award to the claimant or claimants in accordance with regulations enacted pursuant to section four.
source_title: M.G.L. c. 258C, s. 2, Eligibility for compensation

summary: The regulations say sexual assault is, in general, not a circumstance that warrants reducing or denying an award for contributory conduct.
quote: Circumstances that, in general, do not warrant the denial or reduction of an award based on contributory conduct include: 1. acts of negligence or poor judgment such as entering a motor vehicle operated by an intoxicated person; 2. crimes in which the victim is a victim of sexual assault;
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

summary: Victim compensation is available to crime victims, including sexual assault survivors.
quote: Financial compensation from the Victim Compensation and Assistance Division (VCAD) of the Massachusetts Office for Victim Assistance (MOVA) is available to victims of crime, including sexual assault survivors.
pinpoint: MA SANE Protocol, Section X (Victim compensation)
source_title: Mass.gov DPH, MA SANE Protocol Section X: Victim Compensation

summary: A compensable crime must involve force, intimidation or violence, or the threat of it, by the offender against the victim.
quote: provided, however, that such act involves the application of force, intimidation or violence or the threat of force, intimidation or violence by the offender upon the victim.
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

params: {"rule":"Crimes committed in Massachusetts (any victim), plus terrorism abroad against a Massachusetts resident"}
summary: The program covers crimes that happen in Massachusetts, and acts of terrorism outside the United States against a Massachusetts resident.
quote: Crime shall apply to an act occurring within the commonwealth, and to an act of terrorism, as defined in 18 USC section 2331, occurring outside the United States or territories against a resident of the commonwealth.
source_title: M.G.L. c. 258C, s. 1, Definitions

params: {"rule":"A Massachusetts resident harmed in another state may apply only if that state has no compensation program the resident is eligible for"}
summary: A Massachusetts resident victimized in another state is covered only when that state has no compensation program the resident would qualify for.
quote: The word "crime" shall also apply to an act which occurs against a resident of the Commonwealth in a state which does not have a crime victim compensation program for which a resident of the Commonwealth would be eligible.
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

summary: Attach copies of receipts for the expenses being claimed.
quote: Please check types of expenses for which you seek compensation and attach copies of bills and/or receipts.
pinpoint: MOVA Application for Victim Compensation (2026, English), page 3, section 5 (Expenses)
source_title: MOVA Application for Victim Compensation (English)

params: {"document":"itemized_bill","note":"copies of bills and other supporting documentation needed to verify the claim"}
summary: The claim must come with copies of bills and other documents that verify it.
quote: The claim must be accompanied by copies of bills and other supporting documentation necessary to verify the claim
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

params: {"document":"police_report","note":"only when the survivor declined the forensic exam kit or the assault was too long ago for a kit; otherwise a report is not required for exam costs"}
summary: A survivor who declined the forensic exam kit, or was past the kit window, must send a copy of the police report with the application.
quote: In these circumstances, patients must submit a copy of their police report with their Victim Compensation Application.
pinpoint: MA SANE Protocol, Section X (Patient declines MSAECK or patient ineligible for MSAECK)
source_title: Mass.gov DPH, MA SANE Protocol Section X: Victim Compensation

params: {"document":"wage_verification","note":"only when claiming lost wages, and only when MOVA asks; employer verification of employment, dates absent, net weekly earnings and leave used"}
summary: For lost wages, MOVA can ask for the employer's verification of employment, dates missed, net weekly pay and leave used.
quote:
verification from the victim's employer (or, if self-employed, from the victim's own
records) that the victim was employed at the time of the crime
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

params: {"document":"other","note":"disability letter from a treating health care provider, only when claiming lost wages and MOVA asks"}
summary: For lost wages, MOVA can ask for a letter from a treating provider saying the victim cannot work, or can work only part time, because of the crime.
quote:
Upon request by the Agency, the victim must submit a disability letter from a treating health
care provider demonstrating that the victim is disabled from working full time, or limited to
working part time, as a direct result of the crime
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

summary: MOVA says a decision generally comes 4 to 6 months after applying.
quote: In general, you will receive a decision 4 to 6 months later.
pinpoint: Mass.gov, Applying for Victims of Violent Crime Assistance, 'To apply'
source_title: Mass.gov, Applying for Victims of Violent Crime Assistance (MOVA)

params: {"program_name":"Address Confidentiality Program (ACP)","agency":"Secretary of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts","covers_sexual_assault":true,"enroll":"You will need an application assistant to help you. Call 1-866-SAFE-ADD (1-866-723-3233) to find an application Assistant. The application assistant will provide the application and help you complete it. Your application assistant will submit the application to the Address Confidentiality Program. An ACP employee will contact you if your application is approved."}
summary: The Address Confidentiality Program, run by the Secretary of the Commonwealth, protects survivors of sexual assault, rape, domestic violence and stalking who move to get away from the person who hurt them. It is a mail-forwarding service that gives them a protected address to use with state and local agencies, so their new address is harder to find.
quote: The Address Confidentiality Program (ACP) protects survivors of domestic violence, sexual assault, rape, and stalking as well as some legally protected healthcare providers. Survivors often move to get away from perpetrators of violence. The Address Confidentiality Program makes their new address harder to find. The ACP is a mail forwarding service that gives you a protected address to use with state and municipal agencies.
pinpoint: Secretary of the Commonwealth, Address Confidentiality Program page, introduction
source_title: Address Confidentiality Program (Secretary of the Commonwealth program page)

summary: MOVA's regulation says all information it receives or keeps about a compensation claim is confidential and privileged, and anyone who gets those records from the agency may not disclose them.
quote: All information received, obtained or maintained by the Agency in connection with any claim for crime victim compensation shall be confidential and privileged.
source_title: 124 CMR 2.00, Compensation for Victims of Violent Crimes (MOVA; effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564)

summary: When a physician, qualified provider, or hospital gives a rape or sexual offense victim a forensic exam or the related emergency care listed in the statute, the services must be free to the survivor. The statute itself does not mention insurance; the exam billing regulation does.
quote: the services shall be provided without charge to the individual
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-1007 (sexual assault exam payment)

params: {"payer":"Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy, Sexual Assault Reimbursement Unit"}
summary: The provider is paid by the Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy (its Sexual Assault Reimbursement Unit), not by the survivor.
quote: is entitled to be paid by the Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy for the costs of providing the services
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-1007 (sexual assault exam payment)

params: {"payer":"Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy, Sexual Assault Reimbursement Unit","condition":"if done within 15 days of the assault"}
summary: The free-exam rule covers a forensic exam done within 15 days of the assault (or longer if regulation allows) and emergency hospital treatment plus follow-up testing for up to 90 days after the exam.
quote: a physical and sexual assault forensic examination to gather information and evidence as to an alleged crime when the examination is conducted within 15 days of the alleged crime or a longer period as provided by regulation; (2) emergency hospital treatment and follow-up medical testing for up to 90 days after the initial physical examination
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-1007 (sexual assault exam payment)

params: {"payer":"Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy, Sexual Assault Reimbursement Unit"}
summary: The state's reimbursement unit says the forensic exam is covered whether or not the survivor reports to police.
quote: Yes, any victim of sexual assault or rape is entitled to a forensic medical examination regardless of their decision to report sexual assault to police.
source_title: GOCPP: Sexual Assault Reimbursement Unit page and FAQ

summary: A provider may not bill the survivor, the survivor's family, or the survivor's private insurance for any difference between its charges and the state's payment, and must take the state's payment as payment in full.
quote: May not bill a victim of an alleged rape, sexual offense, or child sexual abuse, or the victim's family or private insurance, for any difference between charges and Department reimbursement; and (3) Shall accept the Department's reimbursement as payment in full.
source_title: COMAR 10.12.02 Rape and Sexual Offenses: Physician and Hospital Charges (within COMAR 10.12 full text)

summary: Total compensation is capped at $45,000, including later and supplemental awards.
quote: a total of $45,000, including any subsequent and supplemental awards
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-811 (amount of award)

params: {"exception":"or up to $25,000 more if the injury leaves you fully disabled for life"}
summary: If the injury results in permanent total disability, up to $25,000 more can be awarded after a disability-related claim has been awarded to the victim.
quote: (ii) if the injury to the victim results in permanent total disability, up to an additional $25,000 after a disability–related claim has been awarded to the victim
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-811 (amount of award)

summary: Medical claims are capped at $45,000.
quote: $45,000 for a medical claim
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-811 (amount of award)

summary: Counseling for a person eligible because of psychological injury is capped at $45,000 per claimant.
quote: $45,000 for each claimant for psychiatric, psychological, or mental health counseling under subsection (a)(5) of this section
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-811 (amount of award)

params: {"expense":"counseling","applies_to":"household family members of an injured victim (parent, child, domestic partner, dependent, or spouse living with the victim), not the victim"}
summary: Household family members of an injured victim can get their own counseling, capped at $10,000 per claimant and $20,000 per incident. This cap is for those family members, not for the victim's own counseling.
quote: for an award for psychiatric, psychological, or mental health counseling made under subsection (a)(6) of this section: (i) $10,000 for each claimant; and (ii) $20,000 for each incident
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-811 (amount of award)
set_aside_reason: applies_to "household family members of an injured victim (parent, child, domestic partner, dependent, or spouse living with the victim), not the victim"

summary: Disability-related claims, which is how Maryland pays lost earnings after an injury, are capped at $25,000, with up to another $25,000 for permanent total disability.
quote: for a disability-related or dependency-related claim: (i) except as provided in item (ii) of this paragraph, $25,000
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-811 (amount of award)

summary: Repairing, replacing, or cleaning property damaged by the crime or by the police investigation, including replacing locks, is capped at $2,000 per claimant.
quote: $2,000 for each claimant for repair, replacement, or cleaning of property damaged, soiled, or littered as a result of a crime or law enforcement investigation of a crime, including the cost of replacing locks
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-811 (amount of award)

summary: Funeral expenses are capped at $10,000.
quote: An award for funeral expenses may not exceed $10,000.
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-811 (amount of award)

summary: Medical care and medical supplies count as covered losses.
quote: medical care, including the cost of medical supplies
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-810 (conditions for awards)

summary: Mental health counseling counts as a covered loss.
quote: mental health counseling;
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-810 (conditions for awards)

summary: Lost earnings are covered at up to two-thirds of the victim's gross average wage.
quote: An award for loss of earnings or support made under this subtitle may be up to two-thirds of the victim's gross average wage
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-811 (amount of award)

params: {"expense":"lost_wages","applies_to":"parent or guardian living with a child victim"}
summary: A parent or guardian who lives with a child victim can get up to 30 days of lost earnings for time spent caring for the child.
quote: The parent or guardian of a victim who is a child and who resides with the victim may be eligible for an award of up to 30 days of lost earnings as a result of caring for the victim.
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-811 (amount of award)
set_aside_reason: applies_to "parent or guardian living with a child victim"

summary: A one-time relocation, including a security deposit, counts as a covered loss. No dollar cap for relocation was found in the statute.
quote: the costs of one-time relocation, including any security deposit
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-810 (conditions for awards)

params: {"expense":"transportation","scope":"trips to get medical or mental health care"}
summary: Travel costs to get medical or psychological care count as covered losses.
quote: transportation costs incurred by travel to seek medical or psychological care
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-810 (conditions for awards)

params: {"expense":"childcare","scope":"child care while you get medical or mental health care"}
summary: Child care needed while seeking medical or psychological care counts as a covered loss.
quote: child care expenses incurred as a result of seeking medical or psychological care
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-810 (conditions for awards)

summary: Repairing, replacing, or cleaning property counts as a covered loss, subject to the separate property cap.
quote: repairing, replacing, or cleaning property;
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-810 (conditions for awards)

summary: Replacing locks is covered inside the property cap.
quote: including the cost of replacing locks
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-811 (amount of award)

summary: Eyeglasses and other corrective lenses count as covered losses.
quote: expenses for eyeglasses and other corrective lenses
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-810 (conditions for awards)

params: {"years":4,"from":"discovery","extension":"Child abuse claims can be filed at any time; claims delayed by DNA testing of a sexual assault kit run from notification of the results; the Board can accept late claims for good cause."}
summary: A claim must be filed within 4 years after the crime is discovered, or later in some cases.
quote: a claimant shall file a claim within 4 years after the later of: (i) the discovery of the occurrence of the crime or delinquent act or the death of the victim
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-809 (filing claims)

summary: In a case of child abuse, a claim can be filed at any time.
quote: In a case of child abuse, a claimant may file a claim at any time.
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-809 (filing claims)

params: {"years":4,"extension":"Runs from notification of DNA testing or profile-matching results."}
summary: If filing was delayed because of a delay in testing a sexual assault kit or matching a DNA profile, the 4 years run from notification of the results.
quote: In a case where the filing of a claim was delayed as the result of a delay in the testing of DNA or a delay in DNA profile matching from a sexual assault forensic examination kit or biological material related to a sexual offense, a claimant shall file a claim within 4 years after notification of the results of the testing or DNA profile matching.
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-809 (filing claims)

summary: The Board can accept a late claim if there was good cause for missing the deadline.
quote: A claimant may file a claim at any time if the Board determines that there was good cause for failure to file a claim within the time limits
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-809 (filing claims)

summary: A police report is one kind of evidence the Board must accept. It is not the only one. The Board must also accept medical records showing an injury that fits the crime. It must accept a sworn statement from a qualified third party, and a peace order or protective order. It must also accept any other evidence it thinks helps prove what happened.
quote: The Board shall accept as evidence: (1) a report produced by a law enforcement agency; (2) medical records documenting an injury consistent with the alleged crime; (3) a sworn statement from a qualified third party; (4) a peace order issued under Title 3, Subtitle 15 of the Courts Article; (5) a protective order issued under Title 4, Subtitle 5 of the Family Law Article; and (6) any other evidence the Board considers probative.
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-810 (conditions for awards)

summary: A sexual assault program advocate counts as a qualified third party whose sworn statement the Board accepts as evidence.
quote: an advocate or victim service provider from a domestic violence or sexual assault prevention or assistance program
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-801 (definitions)

summary: The claimant must have at least $100 in unreimbursed expenses, or have lost at least $100 in earnings or support.
quote: The Board may make an award only if the claimant, as a result of the injury on which the claim is based, has: (1) incurred at least $100 in unreimbursed and unreimbursable expenses
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-810 (conditions for awards)

summary: The award is reduced by money from the offender, insurance, workers' compensation, and other public or private sources. Life insurance counts only above a set amount.
quote: An award made under this subtitle shall be reduced by the amount of any payments received or to be received as a result of the injury
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-811 (amount of award)

summary: If the claimant has no private insurance, the program requires applying for Medicaid first.
quote: If the claimant has no private insurance, CICB requires the claimant to apply for Medicaid.
pinpoint: Application instruction sheet, Benefits and Required Documentation
source_title: CICB Application for Crime Victim Compensation with instructions (rev. Nov 2021)

summary: The Board can make an emergency award before deciding the claim if an award is likely and the claimant faces undue hardship. It may not exceed $10,000 and is deducted from the final award.
quote: The amount of an emergency award under this section: (1) may not exceed $10,000
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-813 (emergency awards)

summary: Unless an application is clearly without merit, the Board must make emergency awards for funeral costs, crime scene cleanup, and emergency relocation.
quote: the Board shall make emergency awards for: (1) funeral expenses; (2) crime scene cleanup; and (3) emergency relocation
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-813 (emergency awards)

summary: A victim is anyone who suffers physical or psychological injury from a crime, which includes sexual assault.
quote: who suffers physical or psychological injury or death as a result of a crime or delinquent act
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-801 (definitions)

summary: An award can rest on psychological injury that needed counseling, not only physical injury.
quote: psychological injury to the victim that necessitated mental health counseling
source_title: Md. Code, Criminal Procedure 11-810 (conditions for awards)

params: {"rule":"Crimes in Maryland regardless of residency; crimes elsewhere against Maryland residents"}
summary: Covers crimes committed in Maryland against anyone, and crimes in another state against a Maryland resident.
quote: a criminal offense under state, federal, or common law that is committed in: 1. this State; or 2. another state against a resident of this State

quote: The Program (ACP) was created to conceal the addresses of victims of stalking, domestic violence, sexual assault, human trafficking, and of individuals at risk of being threatened or physically harmed from being located by their perpetrators through public records. ACP provides victims with a designated (substitute) address that can be used instead of their real address.
source_title: Michigan Department of Attorney General: ACP Applicants

summary: The record of a proceeding before the Crime Victim Services Commission is a public record. But a claimant's file and testimony before the commission are exempt from disclosure under Michigan's Freedom of Information Act.
quote: The record of a proceeding before the commission is a public record, except that a claimant's file and his or her testimony before the commission is exempt from disclosure under the freedom of information act
source_title: MCL 18.363 (record of proceeding; claimant's file exempt from FOIA; confidentiality)

summary: A provider may bill the survivor's insurer for a sexual assault exam only if the survivor authorizes it, and may ask for that authorization only after the exam.
quote: The hospital or other licensed health care provider performing the examination may seek insurance reimbursement from the victim's insurer only if authorized by the victim. This authorization may only be sought after the examination is performed.
source_title: Minn. Stat. 609.35 (costs of medical examination)

summary: When asking for that consent, the provider must tell the survivor that the state is required to pay and that the survivor owes nothing and does not have to authorize insurance billing.
quote: the state is required by law to pay for the examination and that the victim is in no way liable for these costs or obligated to authorize the reimbursement
source_title: Minn. Stat. 609.35 (costs of medical examination)

params: {"payer":"State of Minnesota; providers submit exam costs to the Department of Public Safety Office of Justice Programs","condition":"if the crime was in Minnesota"}
summary: The state pays for the exam of a victim of criminal sexual conduct that occurred in Minnesota, including STI tests and treatment and emergency contraception. Providers send the costs to the Office of Justice Programs.
quote: for the examination of a victim of criminal sexual conduct that occurred in the state shall be paid by the state. These costs include, but are not limited to, the cost of the medical forensic examination, associated tests and treatments relating to sexually transmitted infection, and pregnancy status, including emergency contraception. A hospital, emergency medical facility, or health care provider shall submit the costs for examination and any associated tests and treatment to the Office of Justice Programs for payment.
source_title: Minn. Stat. 609.35 (costs of medical examination)

summary: State payment for the exam does not depend on reporting to police or on any investigation or prosecution.
quote: The applicability of this section does not depend upon whether the victim reports the offense to law enforcement or the existence or status of any investigation or prosecution.
source_title: Minn. Stat. 609.35 (costs of medical examination)

summary: Reimbursement to all claimants for one victim's injury or death may not exceed $50,000.
quote: reimbursement paid to all claimants suffering economic loss as the result of the injury or death of any one victim shall not exceed $50,000.
source_title: Minn. Stat. 611A.54 (amount of reimbursement)

summary: The program's own staff training slides list a $7,500 limit for counseling with a licensed provider. The board sets this amount itself, so it can change.
quote: Counseling with licensed provider$7,500
source_title: Financial Assistance for Crime Victims (CVRB training slides, 10/4/2025)

summary: Psychological and psychiatric care needed for the victim's recovery counts as economic loss, up to an amount the board sets.
quote: reasonable expenses incurred for psychological or psychiatric products, services, or accommodations, not to exceed an amount to be set by the board
source_title: Minn. Stat. 611A.52 (definitions)

summary: Lost income is usually paid for up to 26 weeks, with a possible extension of up to 26 more weeks if a physician documents continuing disability.
quote: Compensation for loss of income usually may not exceed 26 weeks. If the victim's disability continues past 26 weeks, the victim may request an extension for up to 26 additional weeks.
source_title: Minn. R. 3050.3200 (loss of income)

summary: The board does not pay for more than 40 missed hours per week.
quote: The board may not compensate for hours missed in excess of 40 hours per week.
source_title: Minn. R. 3050.3200 (loss of income)

summary: Moving expenses, storage fees, and phone and utility installation fees are covered up to $1,000 per claim when the move is needed because of a reasonable fear of danger related to the crime.
quote: the claimant's moving expenses, storage fees, and phone and utility installation fees, up to a maximum of $1,000 per claim, if the move is necessary due to a reasonable fear of danger related to the crime for which the claim was filed
source_title: Minn. Stat. 611A.52 (definitions)

summary: The program's own staff training slides list crime scene cleanup with a $10,000 limit.
quote: scene clean up - $10,000
source_title: Financial Assistance for Crime Victims (CVRB training slides, 10/4/2025)

summary: Child care from a provider exempt from licensing is paid at no more than $3 an hour per child for daytime care or $4 an hour per child for evening care. Licensed facilities are paid up to their standard rate.
quote: Licensed facilities must be paid at a rate not to exceed their standard rate of payment. Facilities exempted from licensing requirements must be paid at a rate not to exceed $3 an hour per child for daytime child care or $4 an hour per child for evening child care
source_title: Minn. Stat. 611A.52 (definitions)

summary: The program's own staff training slides list a $1,500 limit for alternative healing methods such as cultural or religious healing services. The board sets this amount itself, so it can change.
quote: Alternative Healing Methods - $1,500
source_title: Financial Assistance for Crime Victims (CVRB training slides, 10/4/2025)

summary: Necessary medical, hospital, dental, and related expenses, including ambulance and drugs, count as economic loss.
quote: reasonable expenses incurred for necessary medical, chiropractic, hospital, rehabilitative, and dental products, services, or accommodations, including ambulance services, drugs, appliances, and prosthetic devices
source_title: Minn. Stat. 611A.52 (definitions)

summary: Counseling by a licensed provider is covered for victims and their family members.
quote: Counseling expenses by a licensed provider for victims and their family members
source_title: Financial Help for Victims of Violent Crime (brochure, 9/24)

summary: Income the victim would have earned had they not been injured counts as economic loss.
quote: loss of income that the victim would have earned had the victim not been injured

quote: The reparations program reimburses mileage to medical and counseling appointments that are related to the injury from the crime. Miles are calculated from your home address to the clinic/hospital address and are paid at the current federal mileage rate.
source_title: Mileage Reimbursement Request form

summary: Substitute child care or household services the victim would have provided count as economic loss.
quote: reasonable expenses incurred for substitute child care or household services to replace those the victim or claimant would have performed had the victim or the claimant's child not been injured
source_title: Minn. Stat. 611A.52 (definitions)

summary: The board does not reimburse lost tuition, scholarship, or student loan funds, or income lost from delayed schooling.
quote: The board must not reimburse a claimant for loss of tuition, scholarship, or student loan funds or loss of income due to a delay in completion of schooling related to the crime.
source_title: Minn. R. 3050.3200 (loss of income)

summary: Wages already covered by the claimant's paid leave are not paid.
quote: The board must not pay for lost wages covered by a claimant's accumulated sick leave, vacation leave, compensatory time, or holiday pay.
source_title: Minn. R. 3050.3200 (loss of income)

summary: A claim must be filed within three years of the victim's injury. If the claimant was unable to file in that time, the claim can be made within three years of when a claim could have been filed. If the injury could not reasonably be discovered within three years, the claim can be made within three years of when it could be.
quote: no claim was filed with the board within three years of victim's injury or death; except that (i) if the claimant was unable to file a claim within that period, then the claim can be made within three years of the time when a claim could have been filed; and (ii) if the victim's injury or death was not reasonably discoverable within three years of the injury or death, then the claim can be made within three years of the time when the injury or death is reasonably discoverable.
source_title: Minn. Stat. 611A.53 (eligibility and limitations on awards)

summary: These do not count as being unable to file: not knowing about the program, or police not giving you information or help. Being a minor does not count either, and neither does having a parent or guardian handle your affairs.
quote: The following circumstances do not render a claimant unable to file a claim for the purposes of this clause: (A) lack of knowledge of the existence of the Minnesota Crime Victims Reimbursement Act, (B) the failure of a law enforcement agency to provide information or assistance to a potential claimant under section 611A.66 , (C) the incompetency of the claimant if the claimant's affairs were being managed during that period by a guardian, guardian ad litem, conservator, authorized agent, or parent, or (D) the fact that the claimant is not of the age of majority
source_title: Minn. Stat. 611A.53 (eligibility and limitations on awards)

summary: For victims of child abuse, the police report time limit and the minimum claim amount do not apply, and the three-year filing period starts when the crime is reported to police.
quote: The limitations contained in clauses (1) and (6) do not apply to victims of child abuse. In those cases the three-year limitation period commences running with the report of the crime to the police.
source_title: Minn. Stat. 611A.53 (eligibility and limitations on awards)

summary: The crime must be reported to police within 30 days. If it could not reasonably be reported in that time, it must be reported within 30 days of when it could be. A victim of criminal sexual conduct in the first, second, third, or fourth degree who reports after 30 days is treated as having been unable to report within that time.
quote: the crime was not reported to the police within 30 days of its occurrence or, if it could not reasonably have been reported within that period, within 30 days of the time when a report could reasonably have been made. A victim of criminal sexual conduct in the first, second, third, or fourth degree who does not report the crime within 30 days of its occurrence is deemed to have been unable to have reported it within that period
source_title: Minn. Stat. 611A.53 (eligibility and limitations on awards)

summary: The program says there is no time limit to report for sexual assault victims, but the crime must still be reported to police.
quote: Crime must have been reported to police within 30 days (no time limit for sexual assault and child abuse victims, but crime must be reported)
source_title: Financial Help for Victims of Violent Crime (brochure, 9/24)

summary: The victim must cooperate fully with police. Cooperation can be shown by police or prosecutor records, or by a signed document from a victim service, counseling, or medical professional involved in the case. This shows cooperation; it does not replace the police report.
quote: Cooperation is determined through law enforcement reports, prosecutor records, or corroboration memorialized in a signed document submitted by a victim service, counseling, or medical professional involved in the case
source_title: Minn. Stat. 611A.53 (eligibility and limitations on awards)

summary: No award is made if the claim is less than $50; this limit does not apply to child abuse victims.
quote: or (6) the claim is less than $50. The limitations contained in clauses (1) and (6) do not apply to victims of child abuse.
source_title: Minn. Stat. 611A.53 (eligibility and limitations on awards)

summary: Reimbursement is reduced by what collateral sources such as insurance pay, and the claimant must try those sources first.
quote: reimbursement shall be reduced to the extent that economic loss is recouped from a collateral source or collateral sources. Where compensation is readily available to a claimant from a collateral source, the claimant must take reasonable steps to recoup from the collateral source before claiming reimbursement
source_title: Minn. Stat. 611A.54 (amount of reimbursement)

summary: Life insurance and voluntary donations or gifts are not counted as collateral sources.
quote: The term does not include a life insurance contract or benefits from any private source provided as a voluntary donation or gift.
source_title: Minn. Stat. 611A.52 (definitions)

summary: The board may deny or reduce an award for contributory misconduct of the victim.
quote: reimbursement shall be denied or reduced to the extent, if any, that the board deems reasonable because of the contributory misconduct of the claimant or of a victim through whom the claimant claims.
source_title: Minn. Stat. 611A.54 (amount of reimbursement)

summary: The program's own staff training slides say a misconduct reduction may be waived in domestic or sexual assault cases.
quote: May be waived in cases of domestic or sexual assault
source_title: Financial Assistance for Crime Victims (CVRB training slides, 10/4/2025)

summary: The board may grant emergency reimbursement before a final decision when an award is probable and waiting would cause undue hardship.
quote: grant emergency reimbursement pending the final determination of a claim if it is one with respect to which an award will probably be made and undue hardship will result to the claimant if immediate payment is not made
source_title: Minn. Stat. 611A.56 (board duties and powers)

source_title: Financial Help for Victims of Violent Crime (brochure, 9/24)

summary: While a claim is open, the claim and its supporting documents and reports are investigative data. After the claim is paid, denied, withdrawn, or abandoned, they are private data on individuals. The board may still send claim forms, supporting documents, and reports to local law enforcement to carry out section 611A.67.
quote: Claims for reimbursement and supporting documents and reports are investigative data and subject to the provisions of section 13.39 until the claim is paid, denied, withdrawn, or abandoned. summary: In place of other records, the applicant may give a sworn statement under RSMo 589.663 that they have good reason to believe they are a victim of domestic violence, rape, sexual assault, human trafficking, or stalking and fear further violent acts from the assailant.
quote: In lieu of other records the claimant may provide a sworn statement by the applicant under paragraph (c) of subdivision (2) of section 589.663 that the applicant has good reason to believe that he or she is a victim of domestic violence, rape, sexual assault, human trafficking, or stalking, and fears further violent acts from his or her assailant.
source_title: RSMo 595.030 (when paid, maximum award)

summary: To be eligible, you must cooperate with law enforcement in catching the offender, unless the department finds you had good cause not to.

source_title: RSMo 595.015 (claims, application, cooperation)

summary: An award is reduced by payments, benefits, or awards received or to be received because of the injury or death. Life insurance proceeds do not count.

source_title: RSMo 595.035 (reductions, payor of last resort, contributory conduct)

summary: If you have health insurance but still owe deductibles or co-payments, those out-of-pocket costs may be reimbursed.
quote: However, if a claimant has a health insurance but still has out-of-pocket expenses because of deductibles or co-payments, those out-of-pocket costs may be eligible for reimbursement.

summary: The department must consider whether the victim's consent, provocation, incitement or negligence contributed to the injury, and may reduce or deny the award on that basis.
quote: the department of public safety shall determine whether, because of the victim's consent, provocation, incitement or negligence, the victim contributed to the infliction of the victim's injury or death, and shall reduce the amount of the compensation or deny the claim altogether, in accordance with such determination
source_title: RSMo 595.035 (reductions, payor of last resort, contributory conduct)

summary: Sexual assault victims are eligible, and a relative who needs counseling to help the victim recover can also be eligible.

quote: Compensation in cases involving sexual offenses against minors may not be awarded unless the claim is filed with the office within 1 year after the day the criminally injurious conduct was reported to a law enforcement agency or an agency of the state responsible for provision of child welfare services, or within 1 year after the day the victim reaches 18 years of age, whichever occurs last.

summary: A report to a law enforcement officer is required for any award. It must be made within 72 hours, unless the office finds good cause for the delay. The 72-hour limit does not apply to a sexual offense against a minor.
quote: Compensation may not be awarded unless the criminally injurious conduct resulting in injury or death was reported to a law enforcement officer. The report must be made within 72 hours after its occurrence, except in a case involving a sexual offense against a minor or when the office finds there was good cause for the failure to report within that time.
source_title: MCA 53-9-125, Limitations on awards

params: {"required":true,"scope":"what counts as good cause for a late report or claim"}
summary: A state rule lists what can count as good cause for a late report or a late claim. It includes the victim's age when the crime happened and physical or mental incapacity. It also includes a delay that was reasonable given the crime and the injuries, or police or prosecutors not telling the victim about the program.
quote: Factors considered when determining whether "good cause" exists for extending the one-year time limit for filing a claim, or for extending the 72 hour deadline to report criminally injurious conduct to law enforcement after its occurrence include, but are not limited to the following: (a) age of the victim when the crime occurred; (b) whether the delay in filing or reporting was reasonable, considering the circumstances of the crime and the resulting injuries to the victim; (c) physical or mental incapacity; or, (d) failure of law enforcement or prosecutors to notify the victim about the crime victim compensation.
source_title: ARM 23.15.103, Good cause extensions to claim filing and reporting limits (via Cornell LII)

summary: The program pays after insurance and other sources; payments are reduced by what those sources pay or could pay.
quote: Compensation otherwise payable to a claimant must be reduced or denied to the extent the compensation benefits payable are or can be recouped from collateral sources.
source_title: MCA 53-9-125, Limitations on awards

summary: The program is the payer of last resort, but it can pay deductibles and co-pays.
quote: CVC is a payor of last resort. If you are covered by any kind of private or government benefit program, you must submit your expenses to that collateral source before you submit them to the CVC program. CVC benefits can be paid for your out-of-pocket expenses, including any required deductible or co-payment.
pinpoint: Montana DOJ, Crime Victim Compensation page, Insurance and Collateral Sources
source_title: Montana DOJ Office of Victim Services: Crime Victim Compensation

summary: An award may be reduced or denied in proportion to the victim's contribution to the injury.
quote: Compensation may be denied or reduced if the victim contributed to the infliction of death or injury with respect to which the claim is made. source_title: MCA 53-9-125, Limitations on awards

summary: An award may be denied or reduced if the claimant or victim does not fully cooperate with police and prosecutors.
quote: The office, upon finding that the claimant or victim has not fully cooperated with appropriate law enforcement agencies or prosecuting attorneys, may deny or reconsider and reduce an award of compensation.
source_title: MCA 53-9-125, Limitations on awards

summary: A tentative award can be paid early when the claimant faces financial hardship and a final award looks likely. No set amount.
quote: If the office determines that the claimant will suffer financial hardship unless a tentative award is made and it appears likely that a final award will be made, an amount may be paid to the claimant, to be deducted from the final award or repaid by and recoverable from the claimant to the extent that it exceeds the final award.
source_title: MCA 53-9-126, Tentative award of compensation
