summary: Safe at Home is a free program run by the Tennessee Secretary of State. It is open to survivors of rape, sexual battery, or another sex crime, and of domestic abuse, stalking, or human trafficking, who meet its eligibility and application rules. Once approved, you get a substitute address to use as your official mailing address for state and local government.
quote: The Safe at Home Address Confidentiality Program is a statewide address confidentiality program administered by the Office of the Tennessee Secretary of State. It is open to all victims of domestic abuse, stalking, human trafficking, rape, sexual battery, or any other sexual offense who satisfy eligibility and application requirements at no cost. Once a participant has been approved, they are provided with a 'substitute' address that can be used by them and their children as their official mailing address for all state and local government purposes
pinpoint: Secretary of State, Safe at Home FAQ 'What is the Safe at Home Address Confidentiality Program?'; statute T.C.A. 40-38-601 to 40-38-604 (enroll text from 40-38-604(a))
source_title: Tennessee Secretary of State, Safe at Home FAQ: What is the Safe at Home Address Confidentiality Program?

summary: For victims who apply for compensation, Tennessee law makes the home address, home and personal cell phone numbers, Social Security number, and the crime the victim is being compensated for confidential and closed to public inspection. The statute does not list the victim's name or the rest of the claim file.
quote: The following information regarding victims who apply for compensation under the Criminal Injuries Compensation Act, compiled in title 29, chapter 13, shall be treated as confidential and shall not be open for inspection by members of the public: (1) Residential information, including the street address, city, state and zip code; (2) Home telephone and personal cell phone numbers; (3) Social security number; and (4) The criminal offense from which the victim is receiving compensation.
source_title: T.C.A. 10-7-504 (confidential records; (k) Criminal Injuries Compensation Act applicants), 2025 via Justia

params: {"insurance_billing":"unspecified","scope":"the forensic part of an exam or the evidence kit"}
summary: A sexual assault survivor cannot be made to pay for the forensic part of the exam or the evidence kit. The statute does not say whether the survivor's insurance may be billed for it.
quote: A victim of a sexual assault may not be required to pay for: (1) the forensic portion of the forensic medical examination; or (2) the evidence collection kit.
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 56A (Subchapter G, forensic medical examination)

params: {"payer":"Texas Office of the Attorney General, reimbursing the health care provider or sexual assault examiner on application"}
summary: The Attorney General reimburses the provider or examiner for the forensic portion of the exam, the evidence kit, and medical care given during the exam.
quote: a health care provider that provides a forensic medical examination to a sexual assault survivor in accordance with this subchapter, or the sexual assault examiner or sexual assault nurse examiner who conducts that examination in accordance with this subchapter, as applicable, is entitled to be reimbursed in an amount set by attorney general rule for: (1) the reasonable costs of the forensic portion of that examination; (2) the evidence collection kit;
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 56A (Subchapter G, forensic medical examination)

summary: Emergency Medical Care (EMC): the Attorney General pays for medical care given during a sexual assault forensic exam, at medical fee guideline rates, up to $25,000. The program's medical care page treats this as separate from the general award cap.
quote: The attorney general shall make a payment under Subsection (a) in accordance with the medical fee guidelines prescribed by Subtitle A, Title 5, Labor Code. A payment made under Subsection (a) may not exceed $25,000.
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 56A (Subchapter G, forensic medical examination)

params: {"insurance_billing":"unspecified","scope":"the forensic part of an exam or the evidence kit"}
summary: The program's emergency medical care page says victims cannot be billed for the forensic costs of a sexual assault exam.
quote: Note: Victims cannot be billed for forensic costs of the exam.
pinpoint: OAG Emergency Medical Care Compensation page
source_title: OAG Emergency Medical Care Compensation (sexual assault exam)

summary: Awards for one victim and everyone claiming because of that victim's injury may not exceed $50,000 in total.
quote: Except as otherwise provided by this article, awards payable to a victim and any other claimant sustaining pecuniary loss because of injury or death of that victim may not exceed $50,000 in the aggregate.
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 56B (Crime Victims' Compensation)

summary: For crimes after September 1, 2014, counseling is limited to 60 sessions per victim or claimant; more may be approved in unusual circumstances.
quote: for criminally injurious conduct after September 1, 2014, 60 sessions per victim or claimant.
source_title: 1 Tex. Admin. Code 61.503 (Psychiatric Care or Counseling Expenses)

summary: For crimes on or after July 15, 2016, lost earnings are paid up to $700 per week.
quote: On or after July 15, 2016, the maximum amount of an award for loss of earnings is $700 per week.
source_title: 1 Tex. Admin. Code 61.402 (Loss of Earnings)

params: {"expense":"relocation","scope":"moving costs and rent, if the assault happened in your home"}
summary: A victim of sexual assault who was assaulted at home can be paid relocation costs and housing rent.
quote: A victim of stalking, family violence, or trafficking of persons, a victim of sexual assault who is assaulted in the victim's place of residence, or a child who is a victim of a murder attempt in the child's place of residence may receive compensation for the following expenses: (1) relocation expenses, including expenses for rental deposit, utility connections, expenses relating to moving belongings, motor vehicle mileage expenses, temporary or emergency lodging, and for an out-of-state move, expenses for transportation, lodging, and meals; and (2) housing rental expenses.
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 56B (Crime Victims' Compensation)

params: {"expense":"relocation","scope":"moving costs and rent, if a move is needed for your health or safety"}
summary: Other victims can be paid moving costs and rent when a move is needed to protect their health or safety.
quote: A victim other than a victim described by Subsection (c), a dependent of any victim, a family member of any victim if that family member has previously resided with the victim for a period of not less than two years, or a household member of any victim may receive compensation for the following expenses, if the expenses are necessary to protect the health or safety of the victim, dependent, or family or household member: (1) relocation expenses, including expenses for rental deposit, utility connections, expenses relating to moving belongings, motor vehicle mileage expenses, temporary or emergency lodging, and for an out-of-state move, expenses for transportation, lodging, and meals; and (2) housing rental expenses.
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 56B (Crime Victims' Compensation)

summary: Relocation and housing rental expenses together are capped at $5,000 per victim or claimant.
quote: A victim or claimant may not receive more than $5,000 in the aggregate for relocation expenses and housing rental expenses under Subsection (c) or (c-1).
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 56B (Crime Victims' Compensation)

params: {"expense":"temporary_housing","scope":"emergency or temporary lodging for up to 14 days"}
summary: Emergency or temporary lodging can be paid for up to 14 days, as part of help with moving.
quote: Emergency or temporary lodging (up to 14 days)
pinpoint: OAG Rent and Relocation Reimbursement page
source_title: OAG Rent and Relocation Reimbursement

params: {"expense":"transportation","scope":"trips over 20 miles one way to medical or mental health care, court, or a victim's funeral"}
summary: Travel is reimbursed when the one-way trip to medical or mental health care, court, or a victim's funeral is over 20 miles.
quote: Travel over 20 miles one way for medical or mental health care, court proceedings, or a victim's funeral
source_title: OAG Travel Cost Reimbursement

summary: If you were subpoenaed to appear in court, the program does not pay for those trips. Its page says to ask the prosecutor's office instead.
quote: Note: Victims or claimants subpoenaed to appear in court cannot receive reimbursement through the CVC program for those appearances. If subpoenaed, please seek reimbursement from the prosecutor’s office.
pinpoint: OAG Travel Cost Reimbursement page, Note
source_title: OAG Travel Cost Reimbursement

summary: Reasonable and necessary medical, hospital, nursing, and physical therapy costs from the injury are covered.
quote: "Pecuniary loss" means the amount of the expense reasonably and necessarily incurred as a result of personal injury or death for: (A) medical, hospital, nursing, or psychiatric care or counseling, or physical therapy;
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 56B (Crime Victims' Compensation)

summary: For care sought after August 31, 2025, Emergency Medical Care also pays for prescribed care tied to the assault in the 30 days after the exam.
quote: For medical care sought after August 31, 2025, EMC also covers any prescribed continuing medical care that is related to the sexual assault and provided to the victim during the 30-day period following the exam.
pinpoint: OAG Emergency Medical Care Compensation page
source_title: OAG Emergency Medical Care Compensation (sexual assault exam)

summary: Prescriptions and dental work for crime-related injuries are among the medical costs the program lists as covered.
quote: Examples of expenses that can be covered include: Hospitalization Doctor's services Ambulance services Prescriptions Dental work
source_title: OAG Medical Care Expenses

summary: Psychiatric care and counseling are covered losses.
quote: "Pecuniary loss" means the amount of the expense reasonably and necessarily incurred as a result of personal injury or death for: (A) medical, hospital, nursing, or psychiatric care or counseling, or physical therapy;
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 56B (Crime Victims' Compensation)

summary: Lost past and future earnings are covered when caused by the injury, by getting care for it, or by taking part in the investigation or court process.
quote: actual loss of past earnings and anticipated loss of future earnings and necessary travel expenses because of: (i) a disability resulting from the personal injury; (ii) the receipt of medically indicated services related to the disability; or (iii) participation in or attendance at investigative, prosecutorial, or judicial processes
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 56B (Crime Victims' Compensation)

summary: For crimes on or after July 15, 2016, new child or dependent care costs are paid up to $300 per week for each child or dependent.
quote: On or after July 15, 2016, $300 per week for each child or dependent.
source_title: 1 Tex. Admin. Code 61.405 (Other Limits on Compensation)

summary: For crimes on or after July 15, 2016, crime scene cleaning is capped at $2250 per victim.
quote: for criminally injurious conduct that occurs on or after July 15, 2016, compensation may not exceed $2250 per victim.
source_title: 1 Tex. Admin. Code 61.405 (Other Limits on Compensation)

params: {"expense":"clothing_bedding","scope":"replacing clothing, bedding, or property taken as evidence or ruined by the investigation"}
summary: Clothing, bedding, or other property of the victim that police took as evidence or that the investigation made unusable can be replaced.
quote: reasonable replacement costs for clothing, bedding, or property of the victim seized as evidence or rendered unusable as a result of the criminal investigation;
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 56B (Crime Victims' Compensation)

summary: For crimes on or after July 15, 2016, replacement of seized or unusable clothing, bedding, or property is capped at $1000 per victim.
quote: Under Texas Code of Criminal Procedure Article 56.32(a)(9)(G), the OAG may pay for the reasonable replacement costs as follows: (1) for criminally injurious conduct that occurs between September 1, 1995 and July 14, 2016, compensation may not exceed $750; and (2) for criminally injurious conduct that occurs on or after July 15, 2016, compensation may not exceed $1000 per victim.
source_title: 1 Tex. Admin. Code 61.405 (Other Limits on Compensation)

summary: The program does not pay for property theft, damage, or loss. Replacing clothing, bedding, or property seized as evidence or made unusable by the investigation is a separate covered cost.
quote: The CVC Program cannot make payments for the following: Property theft, damage, or loss Identity theft costs Pain, suffering, or emotional distress Any cost not a direct result of the crime
pinpoint: OAG CVC Covered Costs page, Costs Not Covered
source_title: OAG CVC Covered Costs

summary: Pain, suffering, or emotional distress damages are not paid.
quote: The CVC Program cannot make payments for the following: Property theft, damage, or loss Identity theft costs Pain, suffering, or emotional distress Any cost not a direct result of the crime
pinpoint: OAG CVC Covered Costs page, Costs Not Covered
source_title: OAG CVC Covered Costs

pinpoint: OAG Mental Health Care Expenses page
source_title: OAG Mental Health Care Expenses

params: {"years":3,"from":"crime","extension":"or later if you show good cause for the delay"}
summary: Apply within 3 years of the crime; the program can accept a late application for good cause.
quote: You're applying within 3 years of the crime (unless good cause can be shown for the delay).
source_title: OAG CVC Eligibility

summary: If the victim is a child, the time to apply counts from the day the victim or claimant learns of the crime. It ends on the third anniversary of that day, and no later than the child's 21st birthday.
quote: If the victim is a child, the application must be filed not later than the third anniversary of the date the claimant or victim is made aware of the offense, but not after the child attains 21 years of age.
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 56B (Crime Victims' Compensation)

summary: If medical records show the crime left you unable to apply, that time does not count toward the deadline.
quote: If a claimant or victim presents medically documented evidence of a physical or mental incapacity that was incurred by the claimant or victim as a result of the criminally injurious conduct and that reasonably prevented the claimant or victim from filing the application within the limitations period under Subsection (a), the period of the incapacity is not included.
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 56B (Crime Victims' Compensation)

summary: You may not apply unless the crime was reported to police or another public safety agency in a reasonable time. The report cannot be so late that it gets in the way of the investigation and prosecution.
quote: a claimant or victim may not file an application unless the victim reports the criminally injurious conduct to the appropriate state or local public safety or law enforcement agency within a reasonable period, but not so late as to interfere with or hamper the investigation and prosecution of the offense after the criminally injurious conduct is committed.
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 56B (Crime Victims' Compensation)

summary: The attorney general may give more time to report in extraordinary circumstances. The report rule does not apply if the victim is a child.
quote: The attorney general may extend the time for reporting the criminally injurious conduct if the attorney general determines that the extension is justified by extraordinary circumstances. (c) Subsection (a) does not apply if the victim is a child.
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 56B (Crime Victims' Compensation)

params: {"required":false,"scope":"Emergency Medical Care only (medical care at a sexual assault exam), not the full compensation claim"}

pinpoint: OAG CVC Eligibility page, Basic requirements
source_title: OAG CVC Eligibility

summary: The program pays only for losses not covered by a collateral source such as insurance, Medicaid, or restitution.
quote: a claimant or victim suffered personal injury or death that resulted in a pecuniary loss for which the claimant or victim is not compensated from a collateral source.
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 56B (Crime Victims' Compensation)

summary: An award can be denied or reduced if the victim's behavior shares responsibility for the crime, or if the victim did not substantially cooperate with law enforcement.
quote: the attorney general may deny or reduce an award otherwise payable: (1) if the claimant or victim has not substantially cooperated with an appropriate law enforcement agency; (2) if, as a result of the claimant's or victim's behavior, the claimant or victim bears a share of the responsibility for the act or omission giving rise to the claim;
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 56B (Crime Victims' Compensation)

summary: Getting a forensic medical exam is enough to show a sexual assault victim cooperated with the investigation.
quote: a victim receiving a forensic medical examination constitutes sufficient evidence that a victim has substantially cooperated with an investigation of a sexual assault or other sex offense.
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 56B (Crime Victims' Compensation)

summary: An emergency award for urgent costs is possible when a final award is likely and the victim faces undue hardship; it may not exceed $1,500.
quote: An emergency award may not exceed $1,500.
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 56B (Crime Victims' Compensation)

summary: Sexual assault is one of the violent crimes the program covers.
quote: We can help victims of violent crimes or attempted crimes including: Arson (when present in the building) Assault Burglary (when present in the building) Child abuse Criminally negligent homicide DWI crashes Elder abuse Family violence Harassment Hit and run Homicide Human trafficking Kidnapping Manslaughter Robbery Sexual assault
pinpoint: OAG CVC Eligibility page, Covered crimes

summary: The Attorney General runs an address confidentiality program for survivors of sexual assault and other listed crimes. It gives each participant a substitute P.O. box address to use instead of their real home, work, or school address, and forwards their mail.
quote: (a)  The attorney general shall establish an address confidentiality program, as provided by this subchapter, to assist a victim of family violence, sexual assault or abuse, stalking, child abduction, or trafficking of persons in maintaining a confidential address. (b)  The attorney general shall: (1)  designate a substitute post office box address that a participant may use in place of the participant's true residential, business, or school address;
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 58 (Confidentiality of Identifying Information; Address Confidentiality Program, Subch. B)

summary: Texas law keeps your compensation application and the Attorney General's records on it private, with some exceptions. Once compensation is awarded, the name of the victim or claimant and the amount are public under Gov. Code 552.132(c). A court order, your consent, or a subpoena in a criminal case can also open some records.
quote: An application for compensation under this chapter and any information, document, summary, or other record provided to or received, maintained, or created by the attorney general under this chapter, including a report released to the attorney general under Article 56B.054 (f), is: (1)  except as provided by Section 552.132 (c), Government Code, not subject to disclosure under Chapter 552 of that code; and (2)  except as provided by Subsection (c), not subject to disclosure, discovery, subpoena, or other means of legal compulsion for release.
source_title: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. Chapter 56B (Crime Victims' Compensation)

summary: A survivor may not be charged for a medical forensic sexual assault exam, and does not have to take part in the criminal justice system or cooperate with police or prosecutors to get one.
quote: A victim may not be: (a) charged for a medical forensic sexual assault examination; or (b) required to participate in the criminal justice system or cooperate with law enforcement or prosecuting attorneys as a condition of being provided a medical forensic sexual assault examination.
source_title: Utah Admin. Code R270-1, Award and Reparation Standards (effective 12/08/2023)

summary: An exam provider that accepts payment from the Utah Office for Victims of Crime must take it as payment in full and may not try to collect more from the patient.
quote: A sexual assault exam service provider who accepts payment from UOVC agrees to accept that payment as payment in full on behalf of the patient and may not attempt to collect additional payment from the patient.
pinpoint: UOVC Sexual Assault Services Providers billing page, Payment in Full Requirement
source_title: Utah Office for Victims of Crime, Sexual Assault Services Providers billing page

summary: The Utah Office for Victims of Crime may pay the examiner up to $1,250 for a complete medical forensic sexual assault exam with photo documentation; this limit covers the examiner's fee only, and the exam room, lab tests, and medications are paid separately.
quote: The office may pay a medical service provider who performs a medical forensic sexual assault examination: (a) up to $1,250 for a complete medical forensic sexual assault examination with photo documentation
source_title: Utah Admin. Code R270-1, Award and Reparation Standards (effective 12/08/2023)

summary: The office may pay the full cost of medications the exam provider gives the survivor during the exam, such as emergency contraception and medication to treat or prevent sexually transmitted infections.
quote: the full cost of any medications the medical service provider gives directly to a victim during a medical forensic sexual assault examination such as: (i) the morning after pill or high dose oral contraceptives for the prevention of pregnancy; and (ii) medication for the treatment and prevention of sexually transmitted diseases.
source_title: Utah Admin. Code R270-1, Award and Reparation Standards (effective 12/08/2023)

summary: Sexual assault service providers must bill all available insurance or other payment sources before submitting claims to the Utah Office for Victims of Crime.
quote: Providers must bill all available insurance or other payment sources before submitting claims to UOVC.
pinpoint: UOVC Sexual Assault Services Providers billing page, Reminder
source_title: Utah Office for Victims of Crime, Sexual Assault Services Providers billing page

params: {"payer":"Utah Office for Victims of Crime (exam facility fees)"}
summary: The office may also pay the facility where the exam is done 50% of the exam room fee, up to $350, plus the PEHP rate or 50% of the fee for the history and physical, specimen collection, STD and pregnancy testing, and STD treatment.
quote: 50% of the fee for the use of an examination room to perform a medical forensic sexual assault examination up to a maximum payment of $350
source_title: Utah Admin. Code R270-1, Award and Reparation Standards (effective 12/08/2023)

params: {"payer":"Utah Office for Victims of Crime, if the exam provider reports the exam to law enforcement"}
summary: For the office to pay for the exam, the provider who did it must report the exam to law enforcement, and may collect evidence only with the permission of the victim or the victim's legal guardian.
quote: To be eligible for reimbursement of a medical forensic sexual assault examination, the medical service provider who performed the sexual assault forensic examination shall: (a) report the medical forensic sexual assault examination to law enforcement; and (b) only collect evidence with the permission of the victim or the legal guardian of the victim.
source_title: Utah Admin. Code R270-1, Award and Reparation Standards (effective 12/08/2023)

params: {"item":"over-the-counter at-home sexual assault evidence kits and testing of them"}
summary: The office does not reimburse any cost of an over-the-counter at-home sexual assault evidence kit, including the kit and any testing of it.
quote: The office may not provide any reimbursement for any costs associated with an over-the-counter sexual assault evidence kit that is available to the public for at home collection of evidence, including the cost of the kit and the cost of any testing performed on the kit.
source_title: Utah Admin. Code R270-1, Award and Reparation Standards (effective 12/08/2023)

summary: A compensation award may not exceed $25,000, including any award for a secondary victim, except for medical expenses from serious or substantial bodily injury.
quote: Except as provided in Subsection (4)(b), a compensation award may not exceed $25,000 including any compensation award for a secondary victim.
source_title: Utah Code Title 75E, Chapter 5, Office for Victims of Crime (effective 7/1/2026)

summary: An award for medical expenses from serious bodily injury or substantial bodily injury may not exceed $50,000.
quote: A compensation award for medical expenses resulting from serious bodily injury or substantial bodily injury may not exceed $50,000.

summary: A primary victim can get up to 25 outpatient mental health counseling sessions, individual or group. The reparations officer can approve more if the counselor sends enough documentation to justify them and extenuating circumstances call for them.

summary: The current statute says a claim must be filed within three years after the crime.

summary: The requirement that police or court records show the crime was promptly reported does not apply to claims of sexual abuse (which the statute defines to include rape, sodomy, object sexual penetration and sexual battery).
quote: The provisions of this subdivision shall not apply to claims of sexual abuse.

summary: Anyone who submits to and completes a PERK exam is considered to have met the program's reporting requirements.

source_title: Va. Code § 19.2-368.11:1 (Amount of award)

summary: Awards are reduced by payments from the offender or any other public or private source, such as insurance.
quote: Any claim made pursuant to this chapter shall be reduced by the amount of any payments received or to be received as a result of the injury from or on behalf of the person who committed the crime or from any other public or private source
source_title: Va. Code § 19.2-368.11:1 (Amount of award)

summary: The award may be reduced or denied if the victim's conduct contributed to the injury.
quote: the Commission shall determine whether, because of his conduct, the victim of such crime contributed to the infliction of his injury, and the Commission shall reduce the amount of the award or reject the claim altogether, in accordance with such determination
source_title: Va. Code § 19.2-368.12 (Awards; apportionment; reductions)

summary: An emergency award can be no more than $3,000.
quote: the amount of such emergency award shall not exceed $3,000
source_title: Va. Code § 19.2-368.9 (Emergency awards)

summary: Sexual abuse covers rape, sodomy, object sexual penetration and sexual battery.

source_title: Va. Code § 19.2-368.2 (Definitions)

summary: The program lists sexual abuse of minors and adults as an eligible crime, requiring physical injury for misdemeanors or emotional injury for felonies.

summary: The State pays for a sexual assault exam when the survivor has no health coverage or coverage does not pay the whole cost, even if the survivor gets the exam before police or a prosecutor ask for one.
quote: The State shall also bear the costs of sexual assault examinations, as defined in 8 V.S.A. § 4083, administered to victims in cases of alleged sexual assault where the victim obtains such an examination prior to receiving such a request if the victim does not have health coverage or the victim's health coverage does not cover the entire cost of the examination.
source_title: 32 V.S.A. § 1407, Costs to be borne by the State

summary: If the survivor's health coverage leaves a co-payment, coinsurance, deductible, or other cost-sharing for the exam, the Fund pays that share directly to the provider, so the survivor does not owe it.
quote: If the victim's health coverage does not cover all of the medical care provided pursuant to this section and the victim would otherwise be responsible for any co-payment, coinsurance, deductible, or other cost-sharing, the Fund shall pay the victim's share directly to the health care facility or provider.
source_title: 32 V.S.A. § 1407, Costs to be borne by the State

summary: Providers must bill the survivor's health plan, Medicaid, or Medicare for the exam first. If the survivor is uninsured or the plan denies the claim, the Fund pays Vermont providers 60 percent of billed charges and the provider may not bill the survivor for the balance.
quote: Health care facilities and health care providers shall bill the victim's health insurance plan, Medicaid, Medicare, or another health benefit plan, as applicable, for the services described in subsection (b) of this section. If the victim does not have health coverage or if the victim's health benefit plan denies the claim, the Fund shall reimburse health care facilities and health care providers located in Vermont as defined in 18 V.S.A. § 9402 at 60 percent of the billed charges for these claims, and the health care provider or facility shall not bill any balance to the crime victim.
source_title: 32 V.S.A. § 1407, Costs to be borne by the State

summary: Through the CCVS Sexual Assault Program, the initial sexual assault medical exam is covered, including evidence collection, STI and HIV screening and prophylaxis, pregnancy testing, and treatment of related injuries.
quote: Resources are available to pay for the initial sexual assault medical examination to include: collection of evidence STI (sexually transmitted infections) and HIV screening prophylaxis pregnancy testing treatment of related injuries

source_title: 32 V.S.A. § 1407, Costs to be borne by the State

summary: An approved claim can receive up to $10,000 in total, equal to the crime-related losses not paid by other sources.

summary: Prosecution for lewd and lascivious conduct must begin within 6 years, so that is also the time limit to apply for it.

source_title: 13 V.S.A. § 4501, Limitation of prosecutions for certain crimes

summary: For lewd and lascivious conduct against a child under 18, lewd or lascivious conduct with a child, and sexual exploitation of children, prosecution must begin within 40 years. That is also the time limit to apply.

source_title: 13 V.S.A. § 4501, Limitation of prosecutions for certain crimes

summary: For other felonies and misdemeanors, prosecution must begin within 3 years. That is also the time limit to apply.

summary: For a sexual assault that happened in Wisconsin, the Wisconsin Department of Justice pays exam costs directly to the health care provider through the Sexual Assault Forensic Examination (SAFE) Fund. Exam costs are the evidence exam plus testing, prevention and medicine for sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) and medicine to prevent HIV, given or prescribed during the exam. The fund pays only these exam costs, not other medical treatment or follow-up visits. It does not pay if the provider is allowed to bill insurance and the survivor (or a guardian) has reported to police or helped their investigation.
quote: the department shall make an award under this section to a health care provider who conducts an examination to gather evidence regarding a sex offense to reimburse the health care provider only for the examination costs
source_title: Wis. Stat. ch. 949, Awards for the Victims of Crimes (subch. I crime victim compensation; subch. II sexual assault forensic examination compensation)

params: {"payer":"Not the SAFE Fund when the survivor (or guardian) authorizes insurance billing and also cooperates with law enforcement; otherwise the SAFE Fund pays (949.26(1))"}
summary: The SAFE Fund does not pay when the survivor or guardian both lets the provider bill insurance and cooperates with police. If the survivor does not authorize insurance billing, the fund pays the exam costs whether or not they report; if they authorize insurance but do not cooperate with police, the fund pays what insurance does not.
quote: The department may not make an award under this section if, under sub. (2) (b), the health care provider is authorized to seek payment and the victim, or any guardian of the victim, cooperates with a law enforcement agency.
source_title: Wis. Stat. ch. 949, Awards for the Victims of Crimes (subch. I crime victim compensation; subch. II sexual assault forensic examination compensation)

summary: For the forensic exam, no police report is needed: the SAFE Fund may not refuse payment because the survivor does not cooperate with law enforcement or because there is no investigation or prosecution.
quote: The department may not refuse to make an award under this section because the victim or the guardian of the victim does not cooperate with a law enforcement agency regarding the sex offense, or due to lack of an investigation or prosecution of the sex offense.
source_title: Wis. Stat. ch. 949, Awards for the Victims of Crimes (subch. I crime victim compensation; subch. II sexual assault forensic examination compensation)

summary: A crime counts if it was committed or attempted in Wyoming and caused actual bodily injury or actual mental harm.

params: {"rule":"Victims of crimes in Wyoming are covered regardless of residency."}

params: {"rule":"Wyoming residents victimized out of state only if that state has no compensation program."}
summary: A Wyoming resident hurt by a crime in another state is covered only if that state has no crime victim compensation program and the crime would be covered in Wyoming.

params: {"scope":"only information already covered by a confidentiality privilege under Wyoming law"}
summary: By statute, information in victims' compensation claim files and records that is covered by a confidentiality privilege under Wyoming law stays confidential and is not open to public inspection. It is also shielded from legal process and cannot be used as evidence in any proceeding without the consent of the person who gave it.
quote: Information contained in the claim files and records of victims, which are subject to any privilege of confidentiality under Wyoming law, shall remain confidential and shall not be open to public inspection. The information shall be immune from legal process and shall not, without the consent of the person furnishing the information, be admitted as evidence or used for any purpose in any action, suit or other judicial, legislative or administrative proceeding.
source_title: Crime Victims Compensation Act, W.S. 1-40-101 to 1-40-119 (copy posted by DVS)
